title: The Whole Thing at Once
logline: A twelfth-century reservoir so large it was named as a sea, which is not one body of water at all, and which the authorities count as five and as three, both correctly, and which can only be seen either way from the air.
human_question: If the same thing can be honestly counted as five or as three depending on where you stand and how much of it is showing, what am I actually pointing at when I use its name?

place.what_kind_of_place: A very large, very shallow artificial reservoir on the western side of a ruined medieval royal capital in the dry zone, held by an earth bund given as twelve to fourteen kilometres long and twelve to sixteen metres high, depending on the account, pierced by ancient stone sluices that have been repaired and re-fitted many times over. It is not one basin. It was made in the twelfth century by joining separate older reservoirs to each other with narrow channels, and the banks between them still exist: a couple of them surface as low pale lines across the water and become exposed embankments when the level drops. At the southern end the bund runs past a ruined monastic library complex and a colossal rock-cut figure on the shore. The north end sits under the walls of the old citadel, so the water has a ruined city on one shoulder and open dry-zone scrub and paddy on the other.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Scale, and a scale that changes. At full supply it is an inland horizon: twenty-odd square kilometres of water with a flat rim, a metal sheet at sunset, thousands of waterbirds working the shallows, and the towers and dagabas of a dead capital standing in the trees along one shore. Then the dry months take metres off it and the same place becomes a landscape of exposed banks, cracked grey margins, stumps and channels — and the thing that was one sheet of water is visibly three. The bund gives twelve kilometres or more of continuous elevated line to fly and walk, with stone sluices set into it that carry eight centuries of patching in one frame. And the payoff shot is free and repeatable: a high frame that holds the whole of it, in which the joins are visible, which nobody standing on the bank can have.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The water level, on the irrigation year's schedule, and everything that follows it. The reservoir fills through the north-east monsoon and is drawn down through the cultivation season until the shallow arms are mud and the internal banks stand clear. Birds arrive and thin out with the shallows. Sluices are opened and closed and the released water goes out through channels into paddy east of the bund. Light does the rest: the dry-zone haze burns off through the morning and comes back in the afternoon, and at last light the whole sheet goes to metal and then to nothing. None of it is under the crew's control and none of it needs to be.
place.when_it_looks_best: Two trips, and the film needs both. Around February to April, at and after full supply, for the single unbroken sheet, the metal sunsets and the birds. Then August into September, at the bottom of the drawdown, for the exposed internal banks, the cracked margins and the shot in which one sheet of water has become three basins. Early morning for a clear high frame before the haze builds; the hour before sunset for the bund, the sluices and the southern end. Full moon nights are worth a test for the still water and the ruins, but nothing in the film depends on them.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A big-water film with a hard shape to it. An inland sea at dawn with a dead city on its shore; kilometres of earth bund flown end to end; ancient stone sluices opened and water running out into paddy; a hundred thousand birds in the shallows; a metal sunset behind a ruined rotunda and a figure cut out of rock. Then the same place with the water pulled back, cracked mud and old banks standing up out of it, and the final lift that shows what the first shot promised. Someone who never hears a word of the narration gets a complete piece: full, drawn down, and seen whole at the end.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration about counting. The voice never claims anything the frame does not already contain: a name that says sea over a thing that is not one; two counts, five and three, one before and one after two basins were cut off, both invisible from the bank; a drawdown that turns one sheet into three without adding or removing anything; a bank of earth that exists only because heat, cold, water and repair are constantly acting on it; and a lift at the end that names the one reality nothing in the film can show. The chronicle's famous sentence about rainwater is used as evidence of what somebody intended, about another and smaller realm, and then put down. Nobody's greatness is the subject and no engineering is being admired.

sequence.on_screen: First light. The drone lifts off the earth bund on the eastern side and keeps climbing until the frame stops changing: one sheet of water filling the lower half of the image, the towers of a ruined city standing out of the trees on the near shore, and two faint pale lines running out across the water where old banks come up to the surface.
sequence.voice: The name given to this place calls it a sea. It is not a sea, and it is not one body of water either. It was made by joining separate reservoirs to each other with narrow cuts, and those two pale lines are where the banks between them still are. Stand anywhere on the shore and they do not exist.

sequence.on_screen: Higher, and the drone turns slowly so the whole expanse passes through the frame from end to end. Then a hold on one of the necks: a gap in an old submerged bank with water moving through it, weed lying along the current.
sequence.voice: Count the reservoirs that were joined and the answer is five. Count the basins that hold water together now and the answer is three. The same record gives both, one as before and one as after. Neither is a mistake. They are counting the same water at different dates. One name sits on top of both of them.

sequence.on_screen: Down on the bund at water level, lens almost on the surface. A flat horizon, fishing stakes standing in the shallows, egrets working a snag, the far shore a grey line. Nothing in the frame says how many pieces of water are in front of the camera.
sequence.voice: From here neither count is available to you. There is one sheet of water and one horizon and that is the whole offer. The old definition of a mind is nearly as narrow as that. Knowing, always of something, one thing at a time, and never arriving at all unless there is something to know. Whatever is out there, you are handed one of it.

sequence.on_screen: The bund itself: the whole length of piled earth flown end to end in one move, then down among the stone sluices, close on cut stone, brick patching, iron, a modern gate bolted into an ancient opening, water going out through it into a channel.
sequence.voice: The chronicle the monks kept puts one sentence in the mouth of the king whose name this water carries: that not even a little of the water that comes from the rain should reach the sea without first being made useful. He said it before he ruled here, about another, smaller realm. So it is evidence of an intention, and not of this water. It is not a moral, and it did not make him a great man. What is here is this. Earth carried and piled. Stone cut. Holes left in the bank on purpose. These books define physical stuff by what is done to it rather than by what it is — the kind of thing that gets knocked about and altered by heat and by cold. A wall of earth holding water back is that definition with a camera on it.

sequence.on_screen: The dry months. The water has pulled metres back from the tree line: a wide margin of cracked grey mud with stumps in it, heat shimmer. Then the high frame again, and now the sheet is plainly three basins, divided by exposed banks that were underwater in February.
sequence.voice: And here is what decides this count. At full supply this reads as one. Take a few metres off it and the banks come up and it is obviously three. Between the wet months and the dry ones nothing was added to it and nothing was taken away. You could simply see more of it.

sequence.on_screen: Low and slow over one of the necks, following the water through the gap and out the far side in a single unbroken move with no cut in it.
sequence.voice: That was one move over one body of water, and it was not. It was held, let go, held again. These books say something very close to that about a mind, and they say it in two ways that must never be run together. One says a mind is one thing in its general nature and is only divided up so that it can be taught. The other says a being does not have one mind at all, but a run of extremely brief separate ones, too fast and too gapless for anybody to catch the joins.

sequence.on_screen: The southern end. A road running along an embankment, and on the far side of it two shallow depressions with scrub and paddy in them and the outlines of old banks still legible in the ground. A culvert. Nothing dramatic.
sequence.voice: Two of the five are on the other side of that road, and this is a different kind of three. How they came to be left out is told two ways. One account has a repair sending water the wrong way, a dam thrown up to stop it, and the dam becoming a road. The engineers' own record says only that the two were taken off when the reservoir was rebuilt in the last century. Either way, these two were cut off. The map these books hand their student has two totals as well, eighty-nine and a hundred and twenty-one, and they are not like this. They are one set of minds, with the last eight counted again by depth. Nothing was cut off to get from one to the other.

sequence.on_screen: Last light at the southern shore: the ruined rotunda and vestibule of the old library complex, and the great rock-cut figure above the water, both black against a sheet going to metal. Then a slow lift until the whole thing is in one frame again, and a hold until the light has gone out of it.
sequence.voice: Three of the four things these books call real are made. They come together, they hold for a while, they come apart. Everything in this film is that kind of thing, including the name and including both counts. The fourth is not made. It is not this water and it is not the quiet and it is not the dark, and there is no shot of it here or in any film. On the map it is one word, and there is nothing under it that a camera can reach.

concept_merge.why_together: C018 is the concept of a classification held in one view, and the two totals are its whole point: Pradeepika states eighty-one mundane plus eight supramundane making eighty-nine, or a hundred and twenty-one when the supramundane are counted by the five levels of absorption [C018-P:L23–L27], and closes the chapter with a full-page chart that gathers every type into a single frame [C018-P:L33–L56]; Margaya's extract for this concept reaches a hundred and twenty-one from four spheres [C018-M:L125], the same book having already given the four sphere figures and both totals, eighty-nine by the short method and a hundred and twenty-one by the long, in its earlier section on how the mind is divided [C003-M:L5; C003-M:L29], and tells the student to learn the list by heart because further study depends on it [C018-M:L3]. The digest's own reading is that eighty-nine and a hundred and twenty-one are not a disagreement but the same set counted at two resolutions, the eight becoming forty when the depth of absorption is counted as well [C018-P:L23–L25; C018-M:L119–L123]. C003 is what such a map is a map of: mind defined as the knowing of an object, arising only in dependence on an object, taking one object at a time, and running as a beginningless stream of extremely brief moments that passes for a single continuous mind [C003-P:L25; C003-P:L33; C003-P:L31]. C002 is the frame around both: everything falls into four ultimate realities described as activities or forces rather than substances [C002-P:L34; C002-M:L3], materiality being defined by what opposing conditions such as heat and cold do to it [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], three of the four conditioned and impermanent and the fourth not produced at all [C002-M:L21]. This reservoir is the only kind of place where all three are standing in the landscape at once and at a scale one frame can hold: a single name that says sea, a structure whose count depends on how much of it the water is currently showing you, and a documented count of five and of three that differ for another reason: two basins were cut off.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the two totals are not arithmetic and not a textual problem, but a fact about resolution — and that a viewer can watch a resolution change. C018 alone is a list, and its own digest warns that a film which dwells on the numbers becomes a lecture. C003 alone is a definition with nothing to look at. C002 alone is a frame with nothing in it. Put on this water they make the film's best two shots do the argument: the high frame in which the joins are visible and the count is available, and the bank-level frame in which there is one horizon and no count is available at all. The drawdown is the honest version of the concept on this site: one sheet at full supply and three basins at the bottom of the season, with nothing added and nothing removed, which is how eighty-nine and a hundred and twenty-one relate — the same set, the eight supramundane types counted again by depth as forty [C018-P:L23–L25; C003-M:L29]. The five and the three are not that. They are a before and an after, given together by one engineering record, and the difference is that two basins were cut off, whether by a road that began as a temporary dam, as one popular account has it, or in the rebuilding of the middle of the last century, as the record has it. That is subtraction, not resolution, and the film says so rather than letting it stand as an image of the concept. The trio also fixes the ending as a refusal: the unmade reality is not on this map and nothing a camera can reach belongs to it [C002-M:L21; C002-P:L46].

concept_links.why: The concept is the whole classification put in one view together with the fact that it has two honest totals. Pradeepika gives eighty-one plus eight for eighty-nine, and a hundred and twenty-one when the supramundane are counted by the five levels of absorption, with sixty-seven of the hundred and twenty-one being absorption consciousnesses [C018-P:L23–L27], and gathers everything into a single full-page chart at the end of the chapter [C018-P:L33–L56]. Margaya's extract for this concept arrives at a hundred and twenty-one from four spheres [C018-M:L125] — the same book states both totals, eighty-nine short and a hundred and twenty-one long, with the four sphere figures, in its earlier section on how the mind is divided [C003-M:L5; C003-M:L29] — and instructs the student to commit the list to memory because what follows depends on it [C018-M:L3]. This place carries the structure in one respect and not in another. The drawdown carries it: one sheet at full supply and three basins at the bottom of the season, nothing added or removed, only more of it showing. The five and the three do not: they are a before and an after, and the difference is two basins cut off, which is subtraction rather than a change of resolution. Neither count is visible except from the air. Four limits from the digest apply and are written into the risks. The types are momentary kinds of consciousness and not personality types. They are not a ladder of better and worse people, and the chart itself shows many of the higher ones accompanied by equanimity rather than joy [C018-P:L27; C018-P:L56]. The supramundane types are tied to the stages of the path and are not peak experiences anyone can switch on [C018-M:L109–L123]. And the arithmetic is not the point [C018-P:L23–L25]; a film that dwells on it becomes a lecture, which is why the two totals are spoken once, in beat 7, without the arithmetic, and then dropped. The C018 digest notes that the four-sphere sum is not printed in either of this concept's extracts, Pradeepika giving eighty-one plus eight [C018-P:L23] with the derivation of eighty-one before the start of its extract [C018-P:L21]; but the Margaya prints the four figures and both totals in its section on how the mind is divided [C003-M:L29], so there is no gap in the sources for the film to show, and the film does not claim one.

This concept supplies what the map is a map of, and the shot on the bund. Mind is defined as the capacity that knows an object: it arises only in dependence on an object, it takes one object and one aspect of it at a time, and it runs as a beginningless stream of extremely brief moments that feels like a single continuous mind [C003-P:L25; C003-P:L33; C003-P:L31]. That is beat 3, standing at water level with one horizon and no count, and it is beat 6, flying through a neck in one unbroken move over what is not one thing. The digest is explicit that the two sources use 'one' in different senses and that they must not be merged: Margaya says mind is one in its general nature and is divided only for teaching [C003-M:L5], while Pradeepika says a being has not one mind but a stream that merely seems to be one [C003-P:L25]. The film keeps them apart and never lets the aerial settle which sense is meant. Two further limits from the digest bear on this location directly. The author's argument that mind rests on a physical base at the heart rather than in the brain [C003-P:L59–L69] is a commentarial position and must not appear on screen as science. And the ripening simile for resultant consciousness [C003-P:L105–L109] must never be used to explain why a season failed or why any particular field went dry here; the digest rules that out in terms. One further detail earns its place: both sources name the spheres by where such minds 'mostly' arise, not exclusively [C003-M:L11–L19], which is the same loose fit between a name and a plural thing that the reservoir's name has, and the film may note it without pressing it.

This concept gives the film its materiality and its ending. Everything the teaching describes falls into four ultimate realities, described as activities or forces rather than substances and, in Pradeepika's words, as true and existent [C002-P:L27–L30; C002-M:L5; C002-P:L34; C002-M:L3]. Materiality is defined by what opposing conditions such as cold and heat do to it [C002-P:L40; C002-M:L17], which is beat 4: an earth bund and a cut-stone sluice are matter under exactly that description, and Pradeepika's own observation that masses of materiality are what appear to us as trees, rocks and bodies is the ground for a name like sea sitting over an assembled thing. Three of the four are conditioned and impermanent and the fourth is not produced by any cause [C002-M:L21], which is why beat 8 can only name it. The digest's limits are written into the risks and into that beat: it is not relaxation, not a calm mood, not simply death, and it is realised only by noble ones through the supramundane path and great effort [C002-P:L46; C002-M:L21], so still water, dusk and silence are not it. The digest also forbids two slides this film could easily make: 'nothing is real', which Pradeepika's calling the ultimates true existent realities rules out [C002-P:L34], and glossing earth, water, fire and air as literal soil, water, flame and wind, since the extract names the four great elements without defining them [C002-P:L40]. A film standing on an earth dam full of water must not reach for that gloss, and this one does not.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a count is a fact about how much of a thing is showing and how closely you looked, not a fact about how much of it there is. The same water reads as one sheet and as three basins depending on how far it has been drawn down; the same set of mind-moments is eighty-nine and a hundred and twenty-one depending on whether the last eight are counted again by depth. Nothing is added by counting more finely. The five and the three are a different kind of difference — two basins were cut off — and the film says so. The name, which says sea and covers all of it, was never accurate and was never wrong either.
what_must_be_real: Both counts, with their sources, and the reason they differ, told in both of its versions: a popular, uncited account of a nineteenth-century repair that sent water the wrong way and a temporary dam that became a road, and the engineering heritage record's statement that the two basins were taken off in the rebuilding of the 1950s. Neither is narrated as settled. The film records that as layers and does not adjudicate it or turn it into anyone's grievance. The actual state of the reservoir is filmed as it is: siltation, weed, the shallow arms, the condition of the sluices, whatever the level happens to be. No sequence is cut to suggest the water is fuller, or the internal banks clearer, than they were on the day. The chronicle's sentence about rainwater is given as a sentence in a chronicle attributed to a king, spoken about the smaller realm he held before he ruled from this capital, not as the king's own words and not as a statement about this reservoir. People fishing, washing, working the paddy or visiting the ruins are not exhibits, are not filmed in a way that makes them the subject, and are not approached at all where consent cannot be obtained. No chart or table is put on screen as a quotation from a source if the project assembled it.
position_hint: middle: it is the group's change of scale, and the only film in the slate whose subject is a count rather than a thing named. The whole map is laid out here and the later groups open one region of it at a time. No location reasoning is involved.
risks: Letting this become a film about a king's greatness or about medieval engineering genius. The chronicle's sentence is evidence of an intention and nothing more, and the film says so in the beat that uses it.

Letting the arithmetic run the film. The digest states plainly that the numbers are a matter of counting method and that a film which dwells on them becomes a lecture, so the two totals are spoken once, without sums, and dropped.

Claiming a gap in the sources that is not there. The four-sphere figures and both totals are printed together in the Margaya's section on how the mind is divided; any on-screen figure must be one a source prints, and no assembled table is put on screen.

Letting the five-and-three stand as an image of eighty-nine and a hundred and twenty-one. The totals are one set at two resolutions; the five and the three are a before and an after with two basins subtracted. Only the drawdown carries the concept, and beat 7 says so.
Tying the rainwater sentence to this reservoir. The chronicle has the king say it about his earlier, smaller realm, before he ruled from this capital; beat 4 says so.

Reading the types as personality types, as a ranking of better and worse people, or as peak experiences available with a technique; the digest forbids all three, and the chart itself shows many of the higher types accompanied by equanimity rather than joy.

Merging the two senses of 'one'. One source says mind is one in its general nature and divided only for teaching; the other says a being has not one mind but a stream that seems to be one. The aerial must not be allowed to settle that for the sources.

Implying moral causation about water. A low year here is rainfall, siltation and allocation, and the ripening simile in the digest must never be used to explain a failed field or anyone's circumstances.
Letting the last beat imply that still water, dusk, quiet or a ruin is the unconditioned; the digest rules that out and beat 8 is written to refuse it.
Glossing the four great elements as literal soil, water, flame and wind, which is tempting on an earth dam and which the digest explicitly blocks, since the extract names them without defining them.
Presenting the heart-base argument, or any of that author's physiological claims, as established fact.
Turning the separation of the two basins, however it happened, into a colonial-grievance narrative or a nationalist one. Both accounts of it are recorded and left there.

Drone work over a working irrigation scheme, a World Heritage archaeological zone and people fishing, bathing and farming. Permissions are a real constraint and consent for anyone identifiable is not optional.
Crowds and observance at the ruins on the shore. Visitors and worshippers are not spectacle and are not the film's material.
drop_if: The whole reservoir cannot be held in a single frame at a legal and safe drone height, because the first, fifth and last beats are the film.
Drone permission over the archaeological zone and the irrigation works cannot be obtained, and the high frames would have to be bought in or faked.
The internal banks do not become visible at the bottom of the drawdown in the filming year, so the count cannot be seen to change on screen.
The two counts turn out on closer reading to be one authority's error rather than two honest enumerations, which would remove the film's engine.

connections.note: One mountain with four names that are all correct; one body of water with two counts that are both correct. The same distinction between a name and what it covers, taken from naming to counting.
One film lays out a whole map under one name that counts two ways; the other is a shelter lived under for tens of thousands of years by people no name has ever covered.

One body of water counted as one, three and five according to date and water level; two figures held to be a pair and shown by the stones to be centuries apart. Both films keep their counts and datings apart and refuse to pick.

selection.reason: The only idea in which a count, rather than a thing named, is the subject, and the only location where a single name, two documented counts and a structure that shows or hides its own divisions with the water level are all in one frame.

review.note: Confirmed by Chathura on 2026-09-25; reset to pending on 2026-09-26 because a GRP-01 audit corrected voice lines, and decision 9 says a changed body needs judging again. The location is unchanged and has not been reopened; that is Chathura's call. What changed, and why: (1) Beat 7 and the C018 link and merge said one source 'never writes eighty-nine down anywhere' and that the four-sphere sum is 'printed in neither'. That was false: the Margaya's section on how the mind is divided gives 54, 15, 12 and 8 or 40, totalling 89 by the short method and 121 by the long [C003-M:L5; C003-M:L29]. The claim is removed everywhere; beat 7 now says the two totals are one set of minds with the last eight counted again by depth, and the arithmetic recital is cut, as the C018 digest warns. (2) Beat 5 said nothing was added or taken away while beat 7 has two basins taken away; beat 5 now speaks only of the season's drawdown, and beat 7 says outright that the five and the three are a different kind of difference. (3) Beat 4 tied the rainwater sentence to this reservoir; the chronicle (Cv 68.8–12) has the king say it about his earlier, smaller realm before he ruled from this capital, and the voice now says so. (4) Beat 2 said both counts are 'in official print' as if independent; the same engineering heritage record gives them as before and after, and the voice now says that. (5) Beat 7 narrated the nineteenth-century diversion, temporary dam and road as fact; it rests on one uncited popular page, while the ICID record says the two basins were taken off in the 1950s, so the voice now gives both. (6) In the historical thread: the chronicle's own figures (1,471 / 300 / 467 / 1,395) replace the popular 163 / 2,617 / 3,910 / 328 / 168 / 1,969, with all variants kept in what_is_disputed and none averaged; the 'about 386 AD' date for the oldest basin is moved to disputed, with the thirteenth-century Pujavaliya named as the earliest attestation; the chronicle's first Parakkamasamudda, a different reservoir in another district, is recorded; and the bund figures from the ICID record (12.4 km, 15–15.85 m, rehabilitation 1937–1944) are set against the popular 14 km and 12 m. (7) The research note records that the first reference image's GPS tag places it about 55–60 km away. Stale connection notes to IDEA-0006 and IDEA-0012, which described those films' old locations, were rewritten. The audit also recommends reconsidering the location, and says so plainly: no documented story on this site turns on C018, and the film's central analogy is broken, because 89 and 121 are one set counted at two resolutions while five and three are a subtraction. Only the drawdown carries the concept honestly. The one thread worth testing before deciding is the chronicle's several reservoirs with one name (Cv 68.40 and 79.26, and Geiger's note that there may have been more than two): a royal name that does not pick out one body of water. Still unverified: how and when the two basins were actually cut off, the physical dimensions, the true age of the oldest basin, the location of the first image, and every access and drone question.

also_known_as.used_by: one of the three basins counted today

also_known_as.used_by: one of the three basins counted today

also_known_as.used_by: one of the three basins counted today

suggested_location.region: Polonnaruwa District, North Central Province, on the western side of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa; the bund runs along the eastern shore, with the citadel at the northern end and the Potgul Vehera complex at the southern end
suggested_location.why_here: Because the film's argument is here as recorded fact rather than as resemblance. The place is named as a sea and is not one body of water: it was formed by joining separate older reservoirs to each other with narrow channels, and it is counted two ways in print. Five original wewa — Thopa, Dumbutulu, Erabadu, Bhu and Kalahagala — or three interconnected basins today, Thopa, Eramudu and Dumbuthula, because Kalahagala and Bhu were separated from the system — in the 1950s rebuilding according to the ICID heritage record, earlier according to a popular account. Both counts are correct and neither is a mistake, but they are a before and an after: two basins were subtracted. That is not C018's structure, where the tradition counts consciousness as eighty-nine and as a hundred and twenty-one and both are right because they enumerate the same set at different resolutions; what carries that structure here is the drawdown, described below. And the only place either count exists is in the air: from the bund or the shore there is one sheet of water and one horizon, which is the supporting concept's one-object-at-a-time with a camera on it. The reservoir then hands the film a second gift the cascade could not — the count visibly changes with the water. At full supply the internal banks are two pale lines; at the bottom of the drawdown they stand clear and the sheet is plainly three. On top of that it delivers the cinema the brief demands: roughly twenty-two square kilometres of shallow water with a flat inland horizon, an earth bund of twelve kilometres or more to fly, ancient stone sluices carrying eight centuries of repair in one frame, tens of thousands of waterbirds, and a dead capital and a colossal rock-cut figure standing on the shore at last light.
what_to_film: The high frame on a clear early morning, high enough to hold the whole reservoir with the internal banks legible as lines across it. This is beat 1, beat 5 and beat 8, and the film is built around getting it at both water levels.
One of the necks between basins from directly above, then low and slow through it in a single unbroken move with no cut — the shot beat 6 depends on.
Water level on the bund: lens almost on the surface, a flat horizon, fishing stakes, egrets on a snag, nothing in frame to say how many basins are out there.
The bund flown end to end as one continuous line, twelve to fourteen kilometres by different accounts, with the ruined city on one side and paddy and channels on the other.
The stone sluices close up: cut stone, brick and cement patching, iron fittings, a modern gate set into an ancient opening, and water going out through one of them into a channel.
The drawdown: the margin of cracked grey mud with stumps in it, the shallow arms reduced to channels, and the exposed internal banks that make the three basins visible from the ground for once.

The southern end, where a road on an embankment separates the two basins that were left out, with the outlines of their banks still legible in the scrub and paddy beyond it. This is beat 7 and it must not be dramatised.

Last light at the southern shore: the ruined rotunda and vestibule of the Potgul Vehera library complex and the great rock-cut figure above the water, both as silhouettes against the sheet, then the final lift.
Birds in the shallows in numbers, filmed as the place's own scale rather than as wildlife content.
suggested_location.access: Very easy by comparison with most of the slate. The reservoir is immediately west of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa, reached by the Habarana and Dambulla roads, and the bund road runs along its eastern shore past hotels, the citadel and the Potgul Vehera end. Walking the bund and the shore is straightforward. The complications are permissions, not logistics: the ancient city is a UNESCO World Heritage property administered by the Department of Archaeology and the Central Cultural Fund, the reservoir and its sluices are irrigation works under the Department of Irrigation and the Mahaweli authority, and drone flight over a heritage zone needs civil aviation and site clearance. None of that has been sought and all of it should be treated as the main obstacle to the film.
suggested_location.best_time: Two trips. Roughly February to April, at or soon after full supply, for the single unbroken sheet, the metal sunsets and the bird numbers; then August into September, at the bottom of the irrigation drawdown, for the exposed internal banks, the cracked margins and the shot in which one sheet has become three. Early morning before the dry-zone haze builds for every high frame; the last hour of light for the bund, the sluices and the southern shore. The north-east monsoon, roughly October into January, is the filling period and is worth a reconnaissance but is not needed by any beat.

historical_thread.story: On the western side of the twelfth-century capital of Polonnaruwa lies a reservoir whose name declares it a sea: Parakrama Samudra, the Sea of Parakrama, after Parākramabāhu I, who ruled from Polonnaruwa from 1153 to 1186. It is not a sea and it is not one body of water. The northernmost basin, Thopa Wewa, is older than the king: its construction is ascribed to King Upatissa by the Pujavaliya, a thirteenth-century Sinhala chronicle, and by the later Rajavaliya (Geiger, note to Cūḷavaṃsa 37), which is the earliest attestation found; popular pages repeat 'about 386 AD' and the ICID heritage record says the sixth century. What Parākramabāhu is credited with is enlarging the system and tying separate reservoirs together with channels so that they functioned as one storage. The Cūḷavaṃsa describes the work at 79.23–27: the Karaganga dammed and brought in by a great canal to make 'that king of reservoirs' called Parakkamasamudda, 'like to a second ocean', with an island and a palace in it. Geiger's note identifies this reservoir with the Topaveva, 'formerly far more extensive than now' and connected with the Dumbutuluveva to the south, and warns that it is different from the reservoir of the same name at 68.40 — the Pandavapi, today Panda Wewa in Kurunegala District, which the king enlarged while he still held the smaller realm of Dakkhinadesa, before his accession and renamed Parakkamasamudda — adding that there may have been more than two reservoirs called after him. Sources describing the joined system name five wewa: Thopa, Dumbutulu, Erabadu (also written Eramudu, and called Katu Wewa), Bhu and Kalahagala. Sources describing it as it is now name three connected basins: Thopa, Eramudu and Dumbuthula. The ICID heritage record gives both, as before and after, and says Kalahagala and Bhu 'were taken off from the main reservoir in the reconstruction process back in the 1950s'; a popular account (amazinglanka, uncited) says instead that in repairs in the latter nineteenth century water meant for Thopa Wewa began to flow towards Bhu Wewa, that a temporary dam was built to stop it, and that the dam became a permanent road. The ICID record gives a rehabilitation of 1937–1944, a dam 12.4 km long with an average height of 15 m and a maximum of 15.85 m; the popular account gives about 14 km and about 12 m. Along the bund at the southern end stand the ruins of the Potgul Vehera, a monastic complex usually read as a library, and above the water a colossal rock-cut figure. The Cūḷavaṃsa also records the injunction for which the king is best remembered, in Geiger's words 'not even a little water that comes from the rain must flow into the ocean without being made useful to man' (68.11) — but it puts it in a speech about 'the realm that is subject to me', Dakkhinadesa, before he took the throne at Polonnaruwa, not about this reservoir. The chronicle's own count of his works at 79.29–39 is 1,471 small tanks built, stone sluices at 300 tanks, 467 small tanks restored and 1,395 breaches repaired; the larger figures that circulate on popular pages are not from that passage (see what_is_disputed).
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C018's whole point is that a single set of things can be enumerated at two resolutions and that both enumerations are correct: the tradition counts consciousness as eighty-nine and as a hundred and twenty-one, and the difference is only that the eight supramundane types are counted again by the depth of absorption in which they occur, giving forty. Nothing is added by counting more finely, and nothing is lost. On this water the binding is honest in one place and not in another. The drawdown carries it: at full supply the internal banks are two pale lines on the water and the thing reads as one; take a few metres off it and the banks stand clear and it reads as three. Nothing was added or removed; more of it is showing. The five and the three do not carry it. They are a before and an after, and between them two basins were cut off, which is subtraction, not a change of resolution; the film says so in beat 7 rather than offering the pair as an image of the concept. No documented story on this site turns on C018's own question, and that is the weakness of the location. The strongest thread the chronicle offers is a different one: several reservoirs called by one royal name, the chronicle's first Parakkamasamudda being a different tank in another district, so that the name itself does not pick out one body of water. That has not yet been tested as the film's engine. The supporting concepts are bound by the same geometry. From the bund there is one sheet and one horizon and no count is available at all, which is C003's mind that knows one object at a time and runs as a stream that only seems continuous. And the bund itself, earth piled and stone cut and repeatedly repaired, is C002's materiality defined by what heat and cold and water do to it, while the fourth reality can only be named at the end and not shown.
historical_thread.what_is_certain: The reservoir is on the western side of the ancient city of Polonnaruwa and is named as a sea after Parākramabāhu I, who ruled there 1153–1186. It is not a single basin: it was formed by joining separate reservoirs with channels, and the internal banks still exist. Sources naming the five original wewa give Thopa, Dumbutulu, Erabadu/Eramudu (Katu Wewa), Bhu and Kalahagala; sources describing it today give three connected basins, Thopa, Eramudu and Dumbuthula; the ICID heritage record gives both, as before and after. Kalahagala and Bhu are outside the present system. The ICID record gives a rehabilitation in 1937–1944. The Cūḷavaṃsa describes the making of a Parakkamasamudda at Polonnaruwa at 79.23–27, which Geiger identifies with the Topaveva joined to the Dumbutuluveva, and names a different reservoir Parakkamasamudda at 68.40, the Pandavapi. The chronicle's rainwater injunction is at 68.11 in Geiger's translation and is spoken about the king's earlier realm, Dakkhinadesa. The chronicle's figures at 79.29–39 are 1,471 small tanks built, stone sluices at 300 tanks, 467 small tanks restored and 1,395 breaches repaired. The Potgul Vehera ruins and a colossal rock-cut figure stand at the southern end of the bund. The reservoir is inside a UNESCO World Heritage property.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed: The count itself is the film's subject and is left open, but its nature is not in doubt: five and three are a before and an after, not two readings of one state. How the two basins came to be cut off is told two ways and the two are not reconciled: the ICID heritage record says they were taken off in the reconstruction of the 1950s; a popular account (amazinglanka, no source cited) says a later-nineteenth-century repair sent water from Thopa towards Bhu, a temporary dam was built to stop it and became a permanent road. No engineering report has been read that settles it. The physical figures do not agree: the ICID record gives a dam of 12.4 km, average height 15 m and maximum 15.85 m; the popular account gives about 14 km and about 12.2 m (40 ft); Wikipedia gives a surface area of 22.6 km², an average depth of 5 m and a maximum of 12.7 m; the popular account gives 5,350 acres (about 21.6 km²). None of these is averaged. Several reservoirs carried the name: the chronicle's first Parakkamasamudda (Cv 68.39–40) is the Pandavapi, today Panda Wewa in Kurunegala District; Geiger's note to Cv 79.26 says the Polonnaruwa one 'is different from the reservoir of the same name', identifies it with the Topaveva joined to the Dumbutuluveva, and says it is possible 'there were more than two reservoirs called after the King'. The age of the northernmost basin rests on later texts: its construction is ascribed to Upatissa by the thirteenth-century Pujavaliya and the later Rajavaliya (Geiger, note to Cv 37), the earliest attestation found; the date 'around 386 AD' on popular pages and 'the sixth century' in the ICID record are not traced to any source. The figures for his hydraulic works vary and are not from one source: popular pages give 163 major tanks, 2,617 minor tanks, 3,910 channels, 328 stone sluices, 168 sluice blocks and 1,969 breaches repaired, crediting the chronicle; Wikipedia's article on the king gives 165 large tanks, 2,376 minor tanks, 3,910 canals and 163 dams, citing a modern book on the Mahaweli project; the Cūḷavaṃsa itself, at 79.29–39, gives 1,471 small tanks built, stone sluices at 300 tanks, 467 small tanks restored and 1,395 breaches repaired. The Cūḷavaṃsa injunction circulates in several English wordings ('not even a drop of water', 'not even a little water that comes from the rain', 'without benefiting man', 'without being made useful to man'); Geiger's is the second and last, at 68.11, and at least one source notes that the Pali behind 'to man' is rendered in Sinhala as lokopakāra, for the benefit of the world. It is spoken about the king's earlier realm and is not evidence about this reservoir. The identification of the colossal figure at the southern end is itself long disputed — the king, the sage Agastya and others have been proposed — and the film records that it is disputed without adjudicating it and without making the figure or the king its subject.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only. The five original wewa and their names, the three connected basins counted today, both accounts of how two basins were cut off, the rehabilitation dates, the exclusion of Kalahagala and Bhu, the bund length and height, the surface area, depths, catchment and irrigated acreage, and the presence of the Potgul Vehera and the rock-cut figure are from the sources listed above; where figures disagree, the disagreement is recorded in what_is_disputed rather than resolved. The Cūḷavaṃsa passages were read in Geiger and Rickmers's translation on archive.org on 26 September 2026: the rainwater injunction at 68.8–12 (spoken about the king's realm before his accession), the Pandavapi named Parakkamasamudda at 68.39–40 with Geiger's note identifying it as Panda Wewa in Kurunegala District, the Polonnaruwa Parakkamasamudda at 79.23–27 with Geiger's note identifying it with the Topaveva and warning of several reservoirs of the name, the chronicle's own figures at 79.29–39, and the note to Cv 37 giving the Pujavaliya and Rajavaliya as the texts that ascribe the Topaveva to Upatissa. A GRP-01 audit on 26 September 2026 corrected the record's earlier claims that the chronicle gives the figures 163 / 2,617 / 3,910 / 328 / 168 / 1,969, that the rainwater sentence belongs to this reservoir, that both counts are independent official counts, and that the separation mechanism is settled. The coordinates are the reservoir point given in the Wikipedia infobox (7°54′N 80°58′E), rounded, and are an approximate centroid rather than a surveyed position; the bund, the necks between basins, the Potgul Vehera end and the road that cuts off the two abandoned basins have not been located to a coordinate. No engineering or archaeological report on the rehabilitation history has been read, and the ICID record and the popular account of the separation have not been reconciled. Access, drone permission over a World Heritage property and over irrigation works, current water level, siltation, weed cover and the state of the sluices are all unverified. The four Commons images were found through the Commons search API and each file's existence, size and licence short-name were confirmed through a titles query before the URLs were written here; none is an aerial, so the film's decisive high frame is not represented by any verified image. The location of the first image, Parakrama_samudra.jpg, is not confirmed by its metadata: its embedded GPS tag reads 7.54, 80.58, roughly 55–60 km south-west of the reservoir, so either the tag is wrong or the picture is of somewhere else, and its caption should not be relied on until it is checked by eye.

unknowns: No access, permission or local contact has been found or confirmed. Drone clearance over a UNESCO World Heritage property and over active irrigation works is the single largest unknown and could end the film.
Whether the whole reservoir can be held in one frame at a legal drone height, and from where, has not been worked out, and it decides whether the film exists.
Whether the internal banks between the basins are reliably exposed at the bottom of the drawdown, and in which months, has not been checked against irrigation records.

No engineering or archaeological report behind the five-and-three counts has been read. The two accounts of how two basins were cut off — a 1950s reconstruction (ICID) and a nineteenth-century temporary dam that became a road (a popular, uncited page) — have not been reconciled.

The chronicle's injunction is located (Cv 68.11 in Geiger) and belongs to the king's earlier realm; the best rendering of the Pali, and whether any narration should use it at all, still needs an expert reading.
Whether the necks between the basins can be flown low and clean in a single unbroken move, as beat 6 requires, has not been assessed on the ground.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was set by Chathura and is not Claude's to change; its supporting detail is desk research and is unverified, and the historical thread separates what is recorded from what is disputed. No scene or shot is decided here.
